full_judgment:
2. The detenu Kalipada Hazra is the father of the petitioner. It is stated in the petition that the detenu is a Kabiraj by occupation and he was elected as Vice-Chairman of his Union by defeating an influential person of the locality. It is stated that the detenu as an honest and social worker was responsible for securing the arrest of some local dacoits and miscreants in 1974 and 1975, namely, Rabin Biswas, Anil Biswas and Abdul Bari who were arrested by the Police with the help of the detenu it is further stated that the local miscreants who were responsible for various dacoities in the locality became inimical to the detenu and at their behest the detenu was arrested on 29-2-76 and an order of detention was parsed on 2-3-76 under the Emergency Powers Rules, 1975. It is stated further that the detention order is absolutely vague and the detaining authority has not given any material which weighed' in the mind of the detaining authority for passing the order of detention. It is further stated in the petition that the detaining authority had invoked rule 2(e) of the Emergency Powers Rules in justification of passing of the order of detention which, however, does not confer any such power on such authority. It is stated further that the detention is not in accordance with law and therefore, he is being detained illegally and improperly. 

 3. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (General), Jessore has sworn the affidavit on behalf of the respondents and stated that he dealt with the files and records of this case and as such he was well conversant with the facts and circumstances of the case; He admitted that the detenu had been practising as local Kabiraj and had become Vice-Chairman in the year 1973 but added that he could be elected because of the support of the Awami League. It is stated that the fact was not known whether he was an honest social worker and whether he helped the local administration in arresting some dacoits and miscreants in and 1975. It is stated that there was information on record that the detenu was a leader of the gang of criminals and he habitually committed armed dacoity with his partymen. It is further stated that the detention order was passed by the District Magistrate and Deputy Commissioner on 2.3.76 under rule 5(1)(a) of the Emergency Powers Rules as the detaining authority Was satisfied from the materials on record that the detenu had prejudiced and was likely to prejudice the security of Bangladesh public safety and maintenance of public order and "if was necessary to prevent him from doing any such prejudicial act within the meaning of rule 2(e) of the Emergency Powers Rules, 1975". Lastly it was stated that there were sufficient materials on record that the detenu was indulging in political and criminal activity and he did and was about to do prejudicial acts and it is stated that if necessary the relevant records would be produced before the court at the time of hearing. As a point of law it was mentioned that the grounds of detention with the sections of law were mentioned in the order of detention and elaborate discussion was not necessary. Further, it was mentioned that the order of detention was passed "in accordance with provisions of ride 5(1) which almost covered offences defined in rule 2(e)". It was contended that the detaining authority had examined minutely the facts and circumstances of the case with due care and caution before making the order of detention. 

 7. Section 2 of the Emergency Powers Act is quoted below and for the purpose of disposal of this case the following clauses will be relevant: 

 Section 7 as amended inserted 4(1) (a) for punishment under any rules, or any order made under any such rules. The point which requires consideration has been settled by the Pakistan Supreme Court in the cases of Ghulam Jillani and Govt. of West Pakistan Vs. Begum A.K. Abdul Karim,(1967)19 DLR (SC) 403. In that view, it will be convenient if we consider the Defense of Pakistan Ordinance 1965 which it will be seen "has striking similarity both in language and tenor with the Emergency Powers Act. 

 “(X) the apprehension and detention in custody of any person whom the authority empowered by the rules to apprehend or detain, as the case may be suspects on grounds appearing to ' such authority to be reasonable, of being of hostile origin, or having acted, acting, being about to act, or being likely to act in a manner prejudicial to Pakistan's relations with foreign powers, the security, the public safety or interest, or the Defense of Pakistan, or any part thereof, including the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community and the maintenance of peaceful conditions in any area included in Pakistan or prejudicial to The maintenance of public order, or the efficient conduct of military operations or prosecution of war, or with respect to whom such authority is satisfied that his apprehension and detention are necessary for the purpose of preventing him from acting in any such prejudicial manner, the prohibition to such person from entering or residing or remaining in any area, and the compelling of such person to reside and remain in any area, or to do or abstain from doing anything.” 

 was omitted by amendment in 1968 after the decision of Ghulam Jillani's Case repotted in 19 D.L.R. (SC) 403. The Supreme Court held that in terms of section 3 that in order to gain protection for any action the existence of reasonable grounds is essential and mere declaration of satisfaction is not sufficient. It was further held that rule 32 of the Defense of Pakistan Rules owes its vires to section 3(2) 00 and accordingly it was held that by using expression "reasonable grounds" in clause (x) the law has unmistakably reported into this rule, controlling the exercise of public power, the requirement that to gain the protection of the rule for its action thereunder the authority should be prepared to satisfy the courts to which the subject is entitled to have resort for determination of the question whether he has been treated in accordance with law and that he had acted on reasonable grounds. It was further considered that rules 32-and 204 of the Defense of Pakistan Rules were at same par although in rule 204 it was stipulated that the police 'reasonably suspect' and in rule 32 it was 'satisfaction' of the detaining authority. 

 9. Cornelius, C.J. further found that terms of Defense of Pakistan Rules were in identical language of the Defense of India Rules framed under Defense of India Act, 1939. Rule 26 of Indian Rules was in the same language of rule 32 of Pakistan Rules and rule 129 of the Defense of India Rules corresponding to rule 204 of the Pakistan Rules. Cornelius, CJ. further observed that the 'reasonable suspicion' of the Police Officer and the 'satisfaction' of the executive authority has no significance because the conception that was expressed in the case of Shibnath Banerjee by the Privy Council guided by the principle of Liversidge Vs. Anderson was not available for interpretation of the Constitution and the laws of Pakistan inasmuch as under the Government of India Act,1935 "the control by the courts of the exercise of public power by the authorities was at a minimum and the same could not be pressed in service while interpreting the laws of Pakistan. In this view Cornelius, CJ. observed: 

 10. In the case of Government of West Pakistan Vs. Begum A. Karim, (1969) 21 D.L.R. (S.C.) page 1, again the Pakistan Supreme Court considered as to whether detention was illegal. Hamoodur Rahman, J. noticed that in the original section clause (x) was mixed up in two parts-and since in Ghulam Jilani's case this clause has been split up into three parts. In the first part detention was authority and on the basis of the "opinion" of the detaining authority and to it has been added an explanation for the voidance of doubt to the effect that the sufficiency of the grounds on which such opinion as aforesaid is based shall be determined by the authority forming such opinion and the third part dealt separately with temporary detention not upon mere suspicion but upon "reasonable grounds". It was further observed that "rule 32 of Defense of Pakistan Rules is now rentable to amended clause (x) with the explanation and rule 204 is referrable to clause (xc)". After considering the scope of the judicial function Pakistan Supreme Court reiterated the principles that were laid down in the case of Ghulam Jilani's case and endorsed the view "that the amendment of clause (x) of Defense of Pakistan Ordinance has been an exercise in futility. 

 12. The interpretation of the House of Lords in the case of Liversidge Vs. Anderson on the peculiar feature of (he case was not even accepted by the Privy Council in the case of Vimblabai Desphande (A.I.R. 1946 P. C. 123) Its soundness has been doubled in the case of Nakhuda Ali Vs. Jayanton (1951 A.C. 66). Further on examination of the relevant enactment in Ghulam Jilani's case the Supreme Court of Pakistan has shown that the user of expression differently in rules 32 and 204 are without any significance because the 'reasonable suspicion' of a Police Officer and the 'satisfaction' of the Government is at a par in case of consideration of the liberty of the subject when the court is called on to adjudicate the matter. 

 13. It is too late in the day now to canvass that the 'satisfaction' is not justiciable. The reasons which have been given by the Pakistan Supreme Court in Ghulsm Jilani's case (19 D.L.R. SC.403) and in the case of Govt. of West Pakistan Vs. Begum Abdul Karim (21 D.L.R. SC. 1) unmistakably reiterate that satisfaction of the detaining authority when challenged must be proved and section 106 of the Evidence Act is at once attracted and the onus is upon the detaining authority to prove the material 'justification of detention'. To quote again "Having regard to the fact that in such cases the materials upon which the belief is based will be mainly within the special knowledge of the detaining authority and not of The detenu, section 106 of the Evidence Act; it would require the detaining authority to discharge this burden" per Hamoodur Rahman, J in the case of Govt. of West Pakistan Vs. Abdul Karim, (1969) 21 D L R. (SC) 15. 

 14. If the above analysis is cornet then in the Emergency Powers Act and Rules at once the onus is on the detaining authority to show that it had materials. Immediately the question comes whether in the order of detention materials should be given which is relevant to appreciate this contention of Mr. SerajulHuq that the detention order must be indicative of the mind of the detaining authority. He referred to a decision of this court reported in 29 D.L.R., 4 and attempted to argue that the detention order must be speaking order. In that case it was observed: 

 The conception that an order must be speaking order has a legal connotation and the same has been used as far back in 1879 in the case of Overseas of Poor Vs. London Northwestern Railway wherein Lord Cairns observed: 

 Thus it is clear that the speaking order is only related to a proceeding which is to be dealt by way of certiorari. We have not come across any decision that the order of detention must be speaking in the case of habeas corpus. The reasoning is clear because section 106 of the Evidence Act comes into play that it is for the detaining authority to support the detention by way of filing affidavit. In the decisions which were noticed in some of the Dacca High Court decisions it was in the enactment where it was required that grounds are to be supplied because the detenu had a right to file a representation to the Advisory Board. It was a constitutional requirement and therefore the question of supplying the grounds was of importance. To wit sections 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the Special Powers Act required the supplying of grounds for the purpose of enabling the detenu for filing a representation before the Advisory Board and therefore the question when challenged in court as to whether the grounds were vague or indefinite became relevant. But in the Emergency Powers Act having been made in exercise of the proclamation under Article 141A of the Constitution the fundamental rights given in the Constitution were suspended and the right to move the court was also taken away and the provisions for supplying the grounds for making Representation to the Advisory Board, was also done away with it is the Emergency for which the law was accordingly passed. Though the dictum of Lord Atkin in the case of Liversidge Vs. Anderson that "amidst the clash of arms the laws are not silent. They may be changed but they speak the same language in war and peace" has encouraged the superior judiciary in the subcontinent (vide A.I.R. 1964 (SC) 381) yet we would approach this question keeping in mind that "being comes before well-being". 

 Same view was noted in the case of Saleha Begum Vs. Government of Bangladesh, (1977) 29 DLR 59 wherein it was observed: 

 “that by itself in the absence of any specific activity ascribed to the detenu it is not sufficient to bring the case within the scope of prejudicial act as enumerated in rule 2(e) and as such he cannot be described as the miscreant endangering public security no less injuring the interest of People's Republic of Bangladesh.” 

 These observations are based on an erroneous conception and it is unfortunate that the attention of the learned Judges was not drawn to clause (viii) of section 2 of the Emergency Powers Act which empowers the Government for apprehension and detention by application of rule 5(1)(a). When the Government passes the order of detention the law does not empower to take resort to rule 2(e). It is rule 5(1)(a) only and this misconception it seems is persisting amongst the executive because in this case also we found that the executive detaining authority has invoked "rule 2(e) 5(1)(a) of the Emergency Powers Rules, 1975". As has been noted it would not vitiate the order of detention because the detaining authority, has also mentioned rule 5(1) (a). 

 20. Next we come to the contention of the learned Asstt. Advocate General as to the scope and nature of proceeding under section 491 Cr.P. C. The historical background of this section has been detailed by Subha Rao, J in the case of Makhan Singh Vs. Punjab (AIR, 1964 SC. 381). It will be sufficient to note that in 1899 section 491 took away the power of the High Courts of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay to issue writs of Habeas Corpus and empowered them to issue 'directions in the nature of Habeas Corpus subject to limitations. In 1923 by an amendment of section 491 the power to issue directions in the nature of Habeas Corpus was also conferred on other High Courts. Constitution has conferred fundamental rights and Article 102 has empowered the High Court to issue certain writs, inter alia, "so that the court may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner". The High Court is enjoined upon to satisfy itself that the person is not being held in custody (a) without lawful authority or (b) in an unlawful, manner. Hamoodur Rahman, J interpreting the constitutional terms observed: 

 21. Mr. Huq has submitted that while in Constitution the expressions "without lawful authority" or in an "unlawful manner" has been mentioned, the expression in 491 has been used' "illegally or improperly' thereby the legislature has given widest scope for interference to the court in case of illegal or improper detention. 

 23. The expression "whenever it thinks fit" confers an absolute discretion on the court to exercise its power thereunder or not to do so, having regard to the circumstances of each case. While the word "may" used in a statute was sometimes construed as imposing a duty on the authority concerned on whom a power is conferred to exercise the same if the circumstances necessitated its exercise, the expression "whenever it thinks fit" does not warrant any such limitation on its absolute discretion. Though ordinarily a High Court may safely be relied upon to exercise its powers when liberty of a citizen is illegally violated by any authority said unlimited discretion certainly enables it in extraordinary circumstances to refuse, to come to his rescue. The absolute discretionary jurisdiction conferred under S. 491 of the Code cannot be put on a par with the jurisdiction conferred under Art: 326 of the Constitution hedged in by constitutional limitations. Under S. 491 of the Code there is neither a right in the person detained to move the High Court for the enforcement of the fundamental right for there is an obligation on the part of the High Court to give the relief. It is only a discretionary jurisdiction conceived as a check on arbitrary action (A.I.R. SC 413-414). 

 25. Now coming to the affidavit that was filed by the respondents in this case we are constrained to mention that the gentleman who claimed to deal with the files and records of the case has, not practically given any material which would show that at the time of passing of the order of detention there had been application of mind by the detaining authority. It was claimed in paragraph 5 that there was information record that the detenu was a leader of a gang of criminals and further it was stated that the relevant record will be shown to the High Court at the time of hearing in paragraph 8. Further in the affidavit nothing was mentioned as to what are the activities of the detenu in the years 1972, 1973, 1974 and 1975. We have anxiously lookers for the materials and the records which were produced before us but we are constrained to mention again that save and except the fact that the detenu had taken part in the liberation struggle and it is alleged as a member of the political party nothing was mentioned as to how he was indulging in prejudicial activity save and except one point mentioned that the detenu at one time characterised this Government as a carbon copy of Pakistan which again was not taken in affidavit. 

 26. As there are no materials on record to justify the detention, we hold that this is a. case which can be best termed in the celebrated wordings of Hamoodur Rahman, J. against;- 

 27. In view of the above, the opinion is that the detenu is being detained illegally and improperly. In this connection we cannot but voice the opinion that was made by Bose, J. in the case of Ramsingh Vs. Delhi, reported in A.I.R. 1951 (SC) 270 when it was said: 

 “All that is required is that the authorities should bestow on the cases of these detenus a very small fraction of the thought, time and energy which the law compels in the case of even the meanest criminal who is arraigned before the courts of this country.” 

 The fact that there is absent in the cases of these persons all the usual safeguards, the flair of publicity, the right to know with precision the charge against him, the right to speak in -his own defense is all the more reason why Government was to be thoughtful, considerate and kind' and should give them the maximum help. If we may say so we are in agreement with the aforesaid observation of Bose, J, because these detenus are being detained under Emergency Legislation when there is no review by Advisory Board, no scope for filing representation and the matter can only be sorted out when challenged in a court of law and not before that. 

 The Rule is accordingly made absolute. Before parting with this case we acknowledge the assistance that was rendered by both the learned Assistant Advocate General and Mr. Serajul Huq.
